title: Networks (m.net)
text:
m.net.onnela_clustering_coefficient
m.net.onnela_clustering_coefficient(mat)
Weighted clustering coefficient (Onnela et al., 2005).
This is the definition NetworkX computes via nx.clustering(G, weight=...). Unlike clustering_coefficient (which binarizes the input), it uses the geometric mean of each triangle’s edge weights, so weak edges contribute weakly:
w_hat = mat / max(mat)                        # scale by max weight
tri_i = sum_{j,k} (w_hat_ij w_hat_jk w_hat_ki) ** (1/3)
      = diag( cbrt(w_hat) @ cbrt(w_hat) @ cbrt(w_hat) )_i
cc_i  = tri_i / (deg_i * (deg_i - 1))         # deg = unweighted degree
The result is bounded in [0, 1] and reduces to the unweighted clustering coefficient when all edge weights are equal. Assumes a zero diagonal (no self-loops), matching NetworkX. JIT-compatible.

title: Diagnostics (m.diag)
text:
m.diag.ppc_intervals_sorted
m.diag.ppc_intervals_sorted(
    y=None,
    yrep=None,
    x=None,
    prob=0.5,
    prob_outer=0.9,
    title=None,
    name='y',
    x_label=None,
    y_label=None,
)
Predictive intervals with the observations ordered by observed value.
y and yrep default to the model’s observed outcome and its posterior predictive draws (m.diag.get_yrep()); name defaults to the observed site name. For ppc_loo_pit, log_likelihood is computed from the model when yrep is not given.
This is ppc_intervals with observation i placed at the rank of y_i, so the observed points rise from left to right and systematic over/under-prediction across the range of the outcome is easy to read. It performs no leave-one-out computation (ppc_loo_intervals is a deprecated alias).

Type
Description

Observed data.

Posterior predictive matrix.

Inner interval probability (e.g., 0.5).


prob_outer

Outer interval probability (e.g., 0.9).

Plot title. Defaults to one naming the outcome.

Name of the outcome used in the labels.

title: Import Data and handle it
section: Pass a data frame from your session
text:
Pass a data frame from your session
Load, clean, filter or merge your data with the tools of your own language, then hand the data frame to BF; nothing needs to be written to disk. BF works on a copy, so later steps (m.scale(), m.OHE(), …) never modify your original table.

PythonRJulia


import pandas as pd
from BayesForge import bf

m = bf(platform="cpu")

# Any pandas data frame from your session
df = pd.read_csv(m.load.howell1(only_path=True), sep=";")
df = df[df.age > 18]          # e.g. keep adults only

m.data(df)                    # a pandas DataFrame
m.df.head()


library(BayesForge)
m <- importBF(platform = "cpu")

# Any R data.frame from your session (base R, dplyr, data.table, ...)
df <- read.csv(m$load$howell1(only_path = TRUE), sep = ";")
df <- subset(df, age > 18)    # e.g. keep adults only

m$data(df)                    # an R data.frame
head(m$df)


using PyBayesForge, PythonCall, DataFrames, CSV
m = importBF(platform = "cpu")

# Any Julia DataFrame (or other Tables.jl table) from your session
path = pyconvert(String, m.load.howell1(only_path = true))
df = CSV.read(path, DataFrame; delim = ';')
df = filter(:age => >(18), df)  # e.g. keep adults only

m.data(df)                       # a Julia DataFrame
m.df.head()









Tip



Once the data are in BF, select the columns the model uses with m.data_to_model(["weight", "height"]) (list("weight", "height") in R): they become the arrays in m.data_on_model, passed to the model by argument name. See Working with R and Julia tools for getting the posterior draws back as native R or Julia objects.

title: Univariate Linear Regression
text:
Posterior predictive checks
Does the model reproduce the distribution of observed heights?

PythonRJulia




Code
m.diag.ppc_density()


        
        
        


                            
                                            




m$diag$ppc_density()


m.diag.ppc_density()



Each blue curve is the density of one dataset simulated from the posterior; the black curve is the observed heights. The black curve should look like one more blue curve: a shift, a different spread or a different shape (skew, two modes) shows what the model misses. See Diagnostics for every posterior predictive plot.






More checks






PythonRJulia




Code
m.diag.ppc_stat(stat="sd")
m.diag.ppc_loo_pit()


                            
                                            




m$diag$ppc_stat(stat = "sd")
m$diag$ppc_loo_pit()


m.diag.ppc_stat(stat="sd")
m.diag.ppc_loo_pit()



ppc_stat(stat="sd"): the vertical line (observed standard deviation) should fall inside the distribution of simulated standard deviations. ppc_loo_pit: leave-one-out PIT values should be uniform: the observed curve should stay inside the band of uniform curves; a U shape means predictions too narrow, a hump too wide.
